This state file's own 'status' field is constrained by .zoryvex/state.schema.json to PASS/WARN/BLOCKED/PENDING, so the taxonomy bucket is always stated in words inside 'detail' and is authoritative over the enum value. Read this carefully: the PASS/WARN/BLOCKED/PENDING enum is a WORKFLOW-TRACKING field, not an acceptance-evidence field. A row with status PASS whose detail says 'Implemented' has NOT passed a real test — it only means that unit of work is done and not blocking. Never infer acceptance from the enum.

checks.name: CloudFront cache behaviour matches its own stated intent
checks.detail: The static-site module put its 60-second policy on an ordered behaviour matching "*.html" and left Managed-CachingOptimized as the default. Confirmed against live distribution E2ZEO82ZLVJKWW, which had exactly that arrangement. The consequence was smaller than it first reads, and checking rather than reasoning is what established that: sync-static-site.mjs uploads HTML with Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate, CloudFront honours an origin directive over a policy default TTL, and curl against /, /accessibility and /contact returns exactly that header with X-Cache: Miss from cloudfront. So the 24-hour default never applied; the exposure was that correctness depended entirely on the sync script setting that header on every object, with nothing in the distribution behind it. Fixed by making the short TTL the default and scoping CachingOptimized to /_next/static/*, where filenames carry a content hash. terraform-policy-check.mjs now fails if the default is pointed back at the managed policy, verified in both directions. checks.detail: Three corrections and one omission. /for-talent claimed a per-launch-track discovery control that does not exist: a candidate has one launchTrack and one discoveryOptIn flag, which the section below it on the same page already said, and the track argument to setDiscoveryOptIn is a GSI partition key rather than a toggle. The API contract named the session cookie __Host-zoryvex-session while cookies.ts uses __Host-zoryvex_session, introduced when the contract was written and missed because the parity test spelled the name itself rather than reading it from the code; the test now reads it. The employer "what we checked" empty state named two causes and omitted the one that is not the candidate's doing, a lapsed credential. And /how-verification-works, whose entire job is defining what proof means here, never mentioned that a verification expires, which is exactly what makes the word mean something different here from a permanent badge; now documented on the state card, in its own section, and on the Scout tier where an employer decides what they are buying.

checks.name: Auth, deletion, scan and grading paths reviewed and found sound
checks.detail: Recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it. Auth: bounded per-email and per-IP rate limits with a generic error that does not reveal which bound was hit; 256-bit token, keyed-hashed at rest, consumed atomically, identical UnauthorizedError for every failure mode; an existing account keeps its own role regardless of the requested intendedRole, so a code requested as employer cannot promote a candidate; SameSite=Lax is load-bearing because Strict would drop the session on the return navigation from Paystack; the pepper is cached per instance. Deletion deletes its own idempotency guard last, so a retry after partial failure re-runs correctly, and AI explanations live on the match so deleting matches deletes them. A GuardDuty scan result arriving after its file record is gone is a clean no-op rather than a DLQ entry, so deletion cannot manufacture alarms. Graded-task parameters are a pure SHA-256 of candidate and task, so a brief cannot change under a candidate; grading requires identity, score and no disqualifying finding together, with identity outside the score because the pass mark tolerates one miss; a rubric check that throws counts as failed.

checks.name: The Kit checkout screen meets its own acceptance criterion
checks.detail: docs/PRODUCT_SPEC.md requires concrete deliverables, exact limits, final price, seller disclosure and cancellation/refund behaviour before any charge, and docs/ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md repeats it as a Kit-checkout criterion. The screen showed two of the five: price and the Paystack disclosure. The deliverables, the limits and the refund behaviour were absent from the one page where money changes hands. Found by reading the criteria against the page, because the criteria are prose and nothing checks prose. The six deliverables were meanwhile written out literally on two marketing pages and shown nowhere at checkout; they are now one KIT_DELIVERABLES constant rendered by all three, so what a buyer agrees to cannot drift from what they were shown. The refund copy states that refunds are arranged by hand with no automated button, which is what docs/PAYMENTS.md records, and a test fails if it ever starts promising an instant or automatic refund. Also corrected a stale criterion that still called successor pricing "not-yet-authorized" after it was authorized on 2026-08-27 and raised on 2026-08-30. Verified by the employer journey and accessibility specs, 48 passed.

checks.name: Every Lambda is now monitored, for twenty cents a month
checks.detail: docs/RISK_REGISTER.md had carried an open Medium risk since Phase 5: the lambda_errors, lambda_throttles and lambda_duration alarms cover only api and authorizer, so a silent failure loop in any of the other 43 deployed functions surfaced only as a downstream symptom. Closed with two alarms on AWS/Lambda Errors and Throttles with no FunctionName dimension, which CloudWatch publishes as an account-and-region aggregate. Two alarm metrics at $0.10 each, confirmed against AWS's live pricing page and recorded in docs/SOURCES.md, versus roughly $12.90/month to put three alarms on each of the remaining 43. A SEARCH expression was considered and rejected on the same evidence, which contained the finding that changed the design: Metrics Insights alarms bill per metric analysed, so searching 45 functions costs about what 45 alarms cost rather than being a cheap middle ground. The trade accepted deliberately is that these say something failed, not which thing; that was the part missing, and CloudWatch answers the rest in seconds. Per-function alarms stay available as the upgrade if anyone is ever paged often enough to want them.

checks.name: Final end-state verification of what a merge would apply
checks.detail: Bundles rebuilt and re-planned against live TEST at 801833d: 2 to add, 50 to change, 0 to destroy. The additions are the two account-level Lambda alarms. Both deploy guards run clean against that exact plan: hasDangerousDestroy false, detectBlankingRegressions zero findings. Working tree clean, branch in sync with origin, PR #74 mergeable at 16 commits. Local gates green throughout: validate:all 22 steps and 1,146 tests, Playwright 215 passed with 0 failed. Two things remain outside a merge: the founder's one SSM write enabling payments and contactUnlocks in TEST, and live re-verification after the pipeline deploy, which a green CI run does not substitute for.

checks.name: The voice standard is now enforced rather than remembered
checks.detail: CLAUDE.md calls its voice section "a standing bar, not a one-time cleanup", to be applied to every new page, string or component. Nothing enforced it; it held because whoever was writing happened to remember, which is the shape of every other drift found this session. npm run copy:voice now scans the two apps' pages and components, the shared pricing copy and the Kit templates, 79 files, for the banned vocabulary list verbatim and for em dashes in visible prose. Comments are stripped first, because the rule is about how the product speaks and not how the source explains itself. The scan found no banned vocabulary anywhere, which says the copy was genuinely good, and one real em dash in a paragraph on the candidate verification page, now a full stop. Two bugs in the checker were found and fixed before it was trusted: comment stripping collapsed lines so every reported line number was wrong, and the compact-label exemption CLAUDE.md grants ("Item — price") did not survive JSX putting a heading on more than one line, which flagged the exact example the rule names as fine. It exempts short headings and titles, with a length bound so a heading long enough to be a sentence is still checked as one.

checks.name: Four graded-task rubrics marked the more idiomatic answer wrong
checks.detail: The graded tasks are how evidence becomes verified, so a rubric that fails competent work is the most damaging bug here: invisible from the inside, landing on the person least able to argue, while claiming to be objective. Four checks read policy text via rawText(findResources(...)), and findResources filters on type === resource, so a data "aws_iam_policy_document" block was invisible. That is the form the provider documentation recommends and the form this repository's own ci-deploy-role uses; written that way the resource holds only a .json reference and the candidate was told they had not written what they had written. Affected: S3 TLS-only deny, Lambda trust principal, KMS wildcard principal, cross-account sts:AssumeRole. The KMS one failed in the opposite and worse direction, passing a wildcard principal hidden in a data source through the check named for catching it. Fixed with findDataSources in hcl.ts and a policyText helper; the S3 check still requires the bucket policy to exist so an unattached document remains a miss. Three tests, two of them verified to fail against the unfixed grader first. Found by reading one task end to end and asking what a good candidate would actually type, not by any check.

checks.name: The least-privilege task's two security checks were passing the worst answer
checks.detail: Pulling the same thread as the four policy-text rubrics found two more, and these were the serious ones. no_wildcard_action and scoped_resources are the entire point of that task, and both matched on quoted text. rawText only preserves quotes for the jsonencode form, whose body survives as one unparsed expression; the same policy written as an aws_iam_policy_document parses into real strings with the quotes gone, so neither pattern could match it. A submission granting actions ["*"] and resources ["*"] in a policy document passed both checks named for catching exactly that. Fixed with valuesUnderKey, which gathers what a policy grants from either rendering, tested against real values as well as the raw jsonencode body. A bare star fails; an ARN ending in a star still passes, because the brief rules out the unqualified star and not every star, and a test holds that line. Four tests, one verified to fail against the old check first.

checks.name: Seven graded-task rubrics could not read a policy written the recommended way
checks.detail: One blind spot, seven checks, found by reading tasks end to end rather than by any test. A policy written as an aws_iam_policy_document data source was invisible: findResources filters on type === resource, and rawText only keeps quotes for the jsonencode form whose body survives as one unparsed expression. Three failure modes resulted. Missed credit, on the S3 TLS-only deny and the Lambda trust principal, where a candidate was told they had not written what they had written. Security checks passing the worst answer, on the KMS wildcard principal and on the least-privilege task's no_wildcard_action and scoped_resources, where actions ["*"] and resources ["*"] in a policy document walked through the checks named for catching them. And read_only_permissions, which returns false when it finds no actions and therefore failed every candidate using the idiomatic form whether their policy was read-only or not. Fixed with findDataSources in hcl.ts, and policyText, valuesUnderKey and policyActionValues in the rubric module, so every question about a policy is asked of both renderings. An ARN ending in a star still passes, held by its own test. Ten tests added, four of them verified to fail against the unfixed graders first.

checks.name: The demo could not be signed into, and matches were unsorted
checks.detail: Both found by trying to demonstrate the product rather than by reading it. The sign-in form said the demo code was "recorded in the founder/admin view"; no such view exists, and the code was only reachable through developer tools, which the e2e suite uses and a person cannot. The product had a demo mode a non-technical founder could not enter. The code is now shown on the code step, framed as a demo affordance that a real build emails and never displays. Separately, listMatchesForRole returns store order, which is candidate-id order in both localStorage and DynamoDB: the demo store returned scores 0.75, 0.80, 0.60, 0.70, 0.65 in that order and that is what an employer saw. Now sorted strongest first with candidate id breaking ties, on the server and in the demo path, with tests. A first version of that fix quoted misread percentages from a downscaled screenshot; the comment and test fixture now carry the measured values. npm run demo:tour drives the whole product and writes 22 captioned screenshots, so the founder can see what exists without reading code.

checks.name: Standard subscription prices had no code path
checks.detail: The pricing page said the first 25 organizations pay founding prices and everyone after pays standard. Nothing implemented the second half. FOUNDING_SLOTS_TOTAL existed only in apps/web and only to write the number 25 into three sentences; local-payments-adapter held its own copy of the three founding prices, had no copy of the standard prices, and charged founding rates to every subscriber. The 26th organization would have paid 79,000 for the life of its subscription on a page that told it 185,000. subscriptionPrice(plan, placesTaken) in packages/contracts now selects, against a founding-place ledger. Entitlement records priceNGN and foundingMember, stamped at subscription and never recomputed, which is what 'founding members keep their price for the life of the subscription' needed to be true. Two product rules this forced are recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md for founder review: a founding place belongs to the organization and cancelling does not release it, and a checkout quoted at the founding price is honoured even if the last place goes mid-payment.

checks.name: Two price guards were checking last month's prices
checks.detail: assert-safe-shell.mjs proves the neutral export shows no pricing, using a hand-written list of four literals that the 2026-08-30 raise did not update, so the current Kit price and all three standard prices were not checked for at all. It now derives the list from contracts and fails below seven; verified by planting NGN 520,000 in the built output and watching it fail on exactly that. The settlement table in docs/PRODUCT_SPEC.md had no guard: all fourteen figures recomputed correct, so npm run fees:check fixes nothing today and stops the next price change leaving one quietly wrong.

checks.name: Contact unlock was unreachable on the real backend, twice over
checks.detail: unlockContact refuses unless candidate.contactUnlockConsent is true. The API accepts, audits and versions that field; apps/web never shipped a control that sets it and no fixture had it, so every unlock against the real backend would have been refused for every candidate. Separately, matches_unlock_contact_route passed only TABLE_NAME, so getFeatureFlags returned every flag false and flags.contactUnlocks read false on every request: the founder's pending put-parameter to enable unlocks in TEST would have changed nothing. Four more routes had the same gap, including kit_create_order_route, which gates on flags.payments and is the primary launch offer. All five now carry FEATURE_FLAGS_PARAM and an explicit ssm:GetParameter grant in both environments, and npm run flags:wiring fails on either half.

checks.name: The marketplace gate was enforced only in the browser
checks.detail: docs/COMMERCIAL_RUNBOOK.md requires the 5-real-matches eligibility check to pass server-side. The threshold lived in a const at the top of apps/web's role page and nothing in services/api counted matches for any purpose. unlockContact now counts and refuses below MARKETPLACE_GATE_MIN_MATCHES, checked before consent and allowance so an under-supplied role is not reported as a candidate declining. Survivable today only by accident, because subscriptions cannot be bought in real mode so every allowance is zero.

checks.name: Three user-facing statements that were not true
checks.detail: Roles were create-only although PATCH /roles/{id} existed with ownership checks and optimistic concurrency, so a mistyped must-have requirement could only be fixed by buying a second Kit; /employer/role/edit now exists. The evidence visibility option 'Shared with an employer I apply to' described a narrower disclosure than happened (every filter reads visibility !== 'private') and an action the product does not support (no application entity or apply flow exists), and is gone. The candidate's employer preview claimed to be 'exactly what an employer sees' while showing their own name, which employers do not see until they spend a contact unlock.

checks.name: The e2e suite could report green against a stale build
checks.detail: playwright.config.ts used reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI, Playwright's default. A server left from an earlier run answered on 4173, the npm run build in front of it never ran, and a suite that should have failed on a changed match list passed against a build twenty minutes old with nothing in the output saying so. Reuse is off in both places and npm run e2e frees the ports first.

checks.name: The exception queue buried the exceptions
checks.detail: getExceptionQueue returned the fifty most recent audit events, newest first, so a busy hour of ordinary unlocks pushed the one line needing a person to the bottom. `reason` was already the marker without anyone deciding it was: set on a rejected evidence file and on a candidate who was not told their contact had been shared, never on a routine event. Those sort first now. The window is not widened, and the page says so rather than implying a complete list of outstanding items.

checks.name: Accessibility: the claim was true of the pages that had been scanned
checks.detail: /candidate/profile/preview had never been in the axe suite. Adding it found two contrast failures: one added this session, and one there since the page was written (text-ink-500 at 14px on a Card, 4.21:1 against a 4.5:1 minimum). globals.css already documents that exact hazard next to the token and notes it had been caught twice before; this was the third. Every page and component touched or added this session is now scanned. 54 a11y checks pass.

checks.name: The webhook idempotency key was a field most Paystack events do not have
checks.detail: processPaystackWebhook keyed idempotency on payload.data.id and threw when it was missing. data.id is the transaction id: present on charge.success and the dispute events, absent from subscription.create, subscription.disable, subscription.not_renew, invoice.create, invoice.update and invoice.payment_failed, and undefined on subscription.expiring_cards because that event sends data as an array. Every one of those would have returned 500 and been retried by Paystack every three minutes for four attempts then hourly for seventy-two hours, for every such event, indefinitely. The key is now a SHA-256 of the raw body, which is exactly what a Paystack retry redelivers. Found by reading Paystack's current documentation rather than the shapes already in this codebase; the same reading found a charge.failed branch for an event Paystack does not send.

checks.name: Paystack webhooks only fire for successful transactions, so reconciliation is required
checks.detail: Paystack's own words: 'we currently send webhook events for just successful transactions'. There is no charge.failed and no charge.abandoned. A declined card and a closed checkout tab both produce silence, and so does a charge.success whose delivery fails for the full seventy-two hour retry window. A PaymentAttempt row is now written before Paystack is contacted, and an hourly job verifies every attempt that never reached an outcome and separately checks Paystack's recent successes for any with no record here at all. Both directions, because a one-directional reconciliation reports all clear in exactly the case that costs the most.

checks.name: A failed webhook can now be retried instead of alerting a human
checks.detail: The idempotency marker was written before the effect and never removed, so any failure past that line was unrecoverable: the customer charged, the effect half-applied, and every Paystack retry short-circuited as a duplicate. Writing the marker first is still correct — it stops two concurrent deliveries both granting an entitlement. Every effect is now idempotent by construction (conditional status transitions, freshness-guarded writes), so a failure deletes the marker and rethrows, and Paystack's retry genuinely re-attempts. A human is alerted only in the case that is actually stuck: the effect failed and the marker could not be cleared.

checks.name: Paystack does not retry a failed renewal, and docs/PAYMENTS.md said it did
checks.detail: The document's dunning section was built on 'Paystack's own retry schedule runs first'. Paystack's actual words: 'If a subscription charge fails, we don't retry it.' The subscription sits at status attention and the next attempt is the next payment date, a month away. A seven-day grace window now covers that gap: cutting access the instant a charge fails punishes an employer whose card expired over a weekend, and leaving it for the full month gives a month away and calls it dunning. Access is derived on every read rather than stored, so a window that closed twenty minutes ago is closed the next time anybody looks.

checks.name: Three statuses, and a billing page that says what happens next
checks.detail: Payment status, subscription status and access state are separate fields because they answer different questions and change at different moments. The employer-facing page renders all three in words rather than in Paystack's vocabulary and explains the two behaviours nobody would guess: cancelling ends renewal rather than access, and a declined renewal is not retried for a month. The founder's diagnostic keeps the raw Paystack statuses, gateway responses and transaction ids the customer views drop, and states in sentences what is wrong. Neither view can show the subscription email_token: the server strips it before the response is built, and a test asserts the value never appears anywhere in the payload.

checks.name: getEntitlement was discarding the founding price on every real-backend read
checks.detail: priceNGN and foundingMember were added to EntitlementSchema on 2026-08-31 so that 'founding members keep their price for the life of the subscription' had somewhere to be true. employer-repository.ts parsed a hand-listed subset of five fields and was never updated; both new fields carry .default(), so the parse kept succeeding and returned null and false for every employer. The second time a hand-listed projection has silently dropped a field, so the projection now parses the whole stored item, which z.object strips to the schema anyway.

checks.name: Annual billing is modelled, priced by nobody, and therefore not offered
checks.detail: The founder asked for monthly and yearly subscriptions. CLAUDE.md fixes the prices as monthly with no annual plans, and no annual amount has ever been founder-approved. Inventing one would be setting a price rather than making a rounding choice, and a twelve-times multiple is not an annual price. The interval is a first-class dimension through the schema, the plan-key shape, the state machine and reconciliation; OFFERED_BILLING_INTERVALS contains only monthly, and subscriptionAmountNGN throws for anything else rather than returning a number somebody might charge. Recorded as a live founder question in docs/MANUAL_ACTIONS.md.

checks.name: Contact unlocks kept working after a subscription lapsed
checks.detail: getEntitlementPlan returns entitlement.plan and has never looked at entitlement.status, so an organization whose grace window closed kept a plan name and kept spending five contact unlocks a month against it. unlockContact now checks derived marketplace access, and checks it before anything about the role or the candidate: an organization that is not paying should not learn a role's match count or whether a particular candidate consented, because both are things the product sells. Grace still grants, which is the point of a grace window.

checks.name: The Kit was the one paid product reconciliation could not recover
checks.detail: A KitOrder describes a thing that was bought. It cannot describe a charge.success whose delivery failed for the full seventy-two hour retry window, which is exactly the case where the employer has paid and has nothing, and Paystack sends no webhook that would say so. requestKitOrder now writes a PaymentAttempt beside the order, the webhook settles it, and reconciliation recovers it through the same conditional transition the webhook uses, so the two routes cannot both grant.

checks.name: subscription.create defaulted the tier when it could not find the checkout
checks.detail: The default was scout/standard, which would have recorded a Partner founding subscriber as a Scout on the standard price: wrong in both directions at once and invisible until they complained. The tier now comes from the plan-code registry, which is authoritative because Paystack is naming a code this system chose and wrote down, with the payment attempt as fallback and a founder alert rather than a guess when neither resolves. Separately, a renewal charge or a paid invoice landing after a cancel request no longer sets the subscription back to active, which would have shown the employer as subscribed on the page they cancelled from.

checks.name: Six Paystack plans, created by a script that cannot invent an amount
checks.detail: Six plans is six chances to type an amount wrong in a dashboard, and a wrong amount on a Plan bills that number every month for the life of every subscription attached to it. npm run paystack:plans reads the amounts out of packages/contracts rather than carrying its own copy, refuses any key that is not sk_test_, creates only what is missing, refuses to reuse a plan whose amount or interval does not match, and prints the exact aws ssm put-parameter command for the resulting codes. --dry-run shows all six without contacting Paystack. The parse is pinned by its own test, so a rename in the price table fails loudly rather than silently creating nothing and reporting success.

checks.name: Signing out as an employer did not sign you out
checks.detail: EmployerNav cleared local storage and stopped, so on the real backend the httpOnly session cookie and its server record both survived: the next visit, or anyone else on a shared machine, was still authenticated. CandidateNav had always called the real endpoint; AdminNav had the same gap and both admin pages behind it read the real backend. Found by walking every route as a first-time user rather than by running the suite, which is the only way this class of defect surfaces: nothing about it is a logic error.

checks.name: The real role page ranked nothing and offered an unlock it could not honour
checks.detail: The local path sorts matches by score with a comment explaining that neither store returns an order meaning anything; the real path did not, so the mode that charges people for a ranked shortlist was the one serving it unranked. The same page offered Unlock contact on every match with no mention of the five-match marketplace gate, so an employer under the threshold got a button, a click, and a 403 explaining a rule the page had never shown them. Both fixed, and the gate copy no longer hardcodes the threshold in prose.

checks.name: One failed request emptied a list, and one download could silently not happen
checks.detail: The roles list fetched every role's counts under a single Promise.all, so one blip on one role replaced all of them with a 500 page. The data export clicked a detached anchor, which has never reliably worked in Firefox, and revoked the object URL synchronously, which can cancel the download the click just started. The Kit download already got the second half right, with a comment saying why. The export is the one place a candidate exercises a legal right, so it is the worst place for a silent failure.

checks.name: The server's own sentence now survives to the reader
checks.detail: The Kit checkout blamed Paystack for refusals that were nothing to do with Paystack (this role already has a paid Kit, purchases are paused) and told the buyer to try again, which would never have worked. messageFor keeps a 4xx message from the server and uses the caller's fallback for a 5xx, because a 4xx is a statement about this request that will be true again and a 5xx is a statement about a bad moment. Safe by construction: only AppError messages reach a client at all.

checks.name: The threshold was real from the beginning and was never stated
checks.detail: recomputeMatchesForRole writes no match at all for a candidate with no verified evidence supporting a requirement, so somebody with an account, a full profile and nothing checked was invisible to every employer with nothing on their screen saying so. They would reasonably conclude the product was empty rather than that they were outside it. ThresholdPanel names which of the three real conditions is missing: a live proof, the discovery opt-in, or that proof not being private. Each is computed the same way the server computes it, including re-checking a credential's expiry against the clock rather than trusting the stored verified flag.

checks.name: A brand built on what the code already does, and one part deliberately refused
checks.detail: The enemy is "trust me" — a behaviour, not a group — and it is already VERIFICATION_WEIGHT scoring an unchecked claim at zero rather than at a discount. The ritual is the four fields EvidenceSchema has always had, named. The mark dates itself and shows a lapsed proof as lapsed, because a badge implying permanence is a lie about how credentials work. The words are claim and proof rather than evidence, which flattened the one distinction the product rests on. Not built: manufactured belief, which docs/COMMERCIAL_RUNBOOK.md forbids as a dark pattern and which would make this product its own counter-example; and the prophecy, because a brand whose single claim is "don't take a claim on trust" cannot make an unverifiable statement about the future without refuting itself. Recorded in docs/BRAND.md and docs/DECISIONS.md.

checks.name: A live Paystack key could have been pasted into TEST and nothing would have noticed
checks.detail: Dashboard screenshots confirmed the account is live-approved, so a working sk_live_ key exists and can be pasted anywhere a key is asked for. The most expensive mistake available was that key landing in /zoryvex/test/paystack/secret-key, where every automated test, every demo walkthrough and every hourly reconciliation run would have moved real money silently: the environment is decided entirely by which key is configured, with no code branch on environment, which is the right design and exactly why it needed a second opinion. Each environment now declares PAYSTACK_KEY_PREFIX (sk_test_ in test, sk_live_ in production) on every route that reads the key, and getPaystackSecretKey refuses a mismatch. Refusing is the correct direction: a stopped payment is recoverable with one parameter write and a real charge is not. The error names the prefixes, never the key. Also confirmed from the same screenshots: the TEST webhook URL is already set correctly, so that manual action is done.

checks.name: The spec's hard gate on marketplace checkout existed on one side only
checks.detail: docs/PRODUCT_SPEC.md has always said monthly marketplace checkout stays disabled until a saved role has five real, current, discovery-opted matches, and calls it a hard gate rather than a soft nudge. Only half existed: unlockContact refused below the threshold and startSubscriptionCheckout never looked at a match count, so an organization could be sold a subscription while every role it owned was below the line and then find it could not spend a single unlock anywhere. That is a refund rather than a sale, and it is exactly what the rule exists to prevent. Three marketing pages described a per-role checkout gate, which a per-organization subscription cannot be, and which is probably why it was never built: as worded it does not typecheck against the product. The intent is what was implemented — do not sell access nobody can use — so a checkout now requires at least one eligible role, contact details still open per role, and the spec and all four surfaces now say the same thing the code does.

checks.name: Standard prices raised the day before the Paystack plans would have fixed them
checks.detail: Founder decision 2026-09-01: standard Scout 185,000 to 250,000, Team 520,000 to 700,000, Partner 1,350,000 to 5,000,000. Founding held at 79,000 / 229,000 / 599,000 for the third consecutive raise, and the Kit held at 95,000. The timing mattered more than the numbers: a Paystack Plan's amount is fixed on the object once created, no plan objects existed yet and nobody had subscribed, so this was a text edit rather than six new Plan objects and a migration. One source of truth changed and every guard that pins it caught the rest, including fees:check, which refused the settlement table until its nine fee and settlement figures were regenerated from scripts/lib/paystack-fees.mjs rather than edited by hand. Two consequences were flagged to the founder before the change and are recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md: standard Partner is now 7x standard Team where Team is 2.8x Scout, so the tiers must never be described as evenly spaced, and the two price sets interleave, with founding Team cheaper than standard Scout.

checks.name: One standard Partner charge fits inside Paystack's lifetime limit, and the second does not
checks.detail: Found by checking the raise against the provider rather than only against our own tables. Paystack's Nigerian Starter Business lifetime collection limit is NGN 8,000,000, re-verified 2026-09-01 against the current support article (a legacy support2 page still says 2,000,000 and is stale). Standard Partner is NGN 5,000,000, so exactly one charge fits: the subscription cannot take its own first renewal, Paystack neither retries a failed subscription charge nor sends a webhook for one, and the organization would keep access it had stopped paying for until a human noticed. The count is now computed by chargesBeforeLimit in scripts/lib/paystack-fees.mjs, carried per SKU in docs/PRODUCT_SPEC.md, and pinned by npm run fees:check, which was proved to fail by planting a wrong count and by deleting a row. Raising standard Partner took that row from 5 to 1 and nothing would have said so. Lifting the ceiling means becoming a Paystack Registered Business, which requires CAC registration and stays NOT AUTHORIZED BY FOUNDER, so this is recorded as an open founder decision in docs/RISK_REGISTER.md rather than worked around in code.

checks.name: A guard that pins a string can prove agreement with itself, never with the bank statement
checks.detail: The Paystack disclosure named the business as 'Abbas Solution' on every paid surface. The account is 'Abba's Solutions'. The Phase 1 survey on 2026-08-15 misread the dashboard and recorded the misreading as a verified observation; CLAUDE.md's exact-wording rule, the acceptance criterion, PRODUCT_SPEC, the OpenAPI description, V48_BINDING, FOUNDER_READINESS, this file, and the constant six pages render from all inherited it. openapi-schema-parity pinned the string and passed for seventeen days, because it compared our wrong string to our own wrong file. The founder caught it by reading the dashboard, which is the only place it could have been caught. Fixed by extracting PAYSTACK_BUSINESS_NAME as the single declaration, pointing the footer and the trust-and-safety page at it instead of their own copies, and adding apps/web/tests/paystack-disclosure.test.ts, which fails if the name is written out by hand anywhere else under app/ or src/ and was proved by planting one. Historical records were corrected with a dated note that the name was misread rather than renamed; the verbatim COMMERCIAL_RUNBOOK line was deliberately left alone. Nothing was ever charged under either name: no plan, subscription or transaction exists in test or live.

checks.name: Six Paystack TEST plans exist, and Paystack was asked rather than the script believed
checks.detail: Created 2026-09-01 by npm run paystack:plans -- test, on the founder's instruction and after they had moved the dashboard out of Live mode. checks.name: The billing apply has a plan and a rollback, and the rollback had to be captured rather than assumed
checks.detail: Saved plan for the test environment: 45 to add, 55 to change, 0 to destroy. The deploy guards report no stateful destruction and no blanking regressions. The 45 creates are one billing system: four billing routes, the admin billing diagnostic, the hourly reconciliation job (created ENABLED at rate(1 hour)), two CloudWatch alarms, and the empty plan-codes parameter. The 55 changes are mostly not billing: 45 already-running Lambdas get today's code (35 code only, 10 code plus environment), which is the risk-register item about drifted bundles now measured rather than estimated; CloudFront's cache behaviour inverts so pages get a 60-second TTL and only /_next/static/* caches long, which is a correction because the old *.html rule never matched a static export's extensionless paths; and ten functions gain environment variables that exist in code but had never reached AWS. WEBAUTHN_RP_ID looked like a passkey-invalidating change and is not: all four functions currently hold an empty string, so founder step-up has never worked in TEST and this apply is what fixes it. Preparing the rollback surfaced the real hazard: api-route creates functions without publish, AWS keeps only $LATEST, and nothing records which commit built the deployed code, so the 45 code overwrites are irreversible from AWS. All 45 live packages were therefore downloaded and hash-verified against CodeSha256 twice by two separate code paths, every archive opened to prove it is not truncated, alongside the exact pre-apply state version, the CloudFront config and six IAM policies. scripts/capture-rollback-artifact.mjs makes that repeatable and refuses to record an unverified copy. Not exercised, and said so: the restore itself, because running update-function-code to prove a rollback works is the deployment the rollback exists to protect against. Also recorded: /zoryvex/test/last-good-commit does not exist, so the automatic app-code rollback has no anchor for this apply and the captured artifact is the rollback. Nothing has been applied.

checks.name: The deploy script could not finish on Windows, and only a real apply could have found it
checks.detail: terraform apply succeeded and the deploy then died on spawnSync npm ENOENT, between the apply and the site sync: infrastructure changed, site not synced, smoke test never run, last-good commit never recorded, and the automatic rollback correctly failed because no anchor existed. npm on Windows is a .cmd shim, so execFileSync('npm') raises ENOENT and blames npm rather than the shell. Mapping to npm.cmd produced EINVAL instead, because Node refuses .cmd and .bat without a shell since the 2024 argument-injection hardening. Two failures at the same step is the stop-guessing line, so the third attempt ran all four combinations in isolation first and confirmed only npm.cmd with shell:true works. Because a shell concatenates rather than escapes arguments, spawnPlanFor refuses any argument carrying a space or metacharacter instead of attempting Windows quoting that would be exercised rarely and wrong when it mattered. Six tests pin it, including that nothing changes on linux and darwin where CI runs. The bug was unreachable from validate:all, the unit suite and the e2e suite, none of which run deploy.mjs, and the script's header claimed end-to-end use that predated the site-build step.

checks.name: The repository and TEST looked in exact parity, and the measurement was platform-relative
checks.detail: The longest-standing open risk in the register was that Lambda bundles on disk differed from what is deployed, so any future apply would carry a code deployment with it. It was closed by shipping them deliberately with a captured rollback, rather than by continuing to name them. Proved twice over: a plan-only run after the final deploy reports +0 ~0 -0, and the reconciliation function's deployed CodeSha256 compares byte-identical to the local bundle. Keeping it closed is the job of running a deploy after a merge, which is now possible on this machine for the first time, since scripts/deploy.mjs could not complete on Windows until today. The deploy also reports the live feature-flag document matching Terraform, so the two kinds of drift this project tracks are both at zero. CORRECTED 2026-09-01, later the same day: both measurements were taken on the machine that built the bundles, and neither meant what it was read to mean. The first CI deploy on the same commit planned +0 ~53 -0, and a local rebuild and plan immediately afterwards planned the same 53 back. Zip builds are deterministic on one platform and not across two, so a Windows-built and a Linux-built bundle of identical source hash differently. Nothing is broken by it and no data is at risk; what is lost is the signal, since a plan showing 53 changes meant only which machine ran it. The rule from here is the one slice 9 already wrote down: TEST is deployed by CI, not from a workstation.

checks.name: Location filters matches, and the filter says what it costs
checks.detail: Founder decision closing the fork open since the day's first message: location filters rather than merely informs. Role.constraints was free text hinted 'Location, timezone overlap, start date' that no code read, and the seeded roles saying 'Remote, Nigeria-based' and 'overlapping 4 hours with WAT' filtered nobody; candidates had no location field to filter against either. Now a candidate states a country and a working UTC offset, and a role states an allow-list of countries plus a maximum timezone distance from its own offset. Four choices recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md because each could have gone the other way: an allow-list and never a deny-list, since the two are the same arithmetic and only one stays a payroll question; location stated and never inferred, since an inferred location turns a payroll filter into a proxy for nationality; a candidate with no stated location never excluded, since dropping them would be a silent rejection caused by a schema change; and the filter reporting how many candidates it removed, since a shortlist that quietly got shorter looks like a platform with nobody on it. An already-unlocked match that stops fitting is kept rather than deleted or hidden, because it is the record of a purchase, and its rationale says why it no longer fits. 26 new tests across the pure fit function, the matcher, and the profile service, including the clock-wraparound case where UTC+13 and UTC-11 are the same time rather than 24 hours apart, and the null-versus-undefined case where clearing a location must REMOVE the attribute rather than store a DynamoDB NULL that the schema would then reject on read. The openapi parity guard caught both new fields missing from the document. Known limitation recorded rather than buried: a stored offset is not a timezone, so a DST region is an hour out for part of the year.

checks.name: The first CI deploy failed closed on a permission the billing work never granted
checks.detail: PR #74 merged to main as 51d02db and deploy-test failed. Cause read from the log rather than guessed: AccessDeniedException, assumed-role/zoryvex-test-deploy is not authorized for ssm:GetParameter on /zoryvex/test/paystack/plan-codes. The CI role's read grant is a list of exact literal parameter names rather than the /zoryvex/test/* namespace, deliberately, because the Paystack secret key sits under that same prefix and the role can write to it. Today's billing work added a third parameter to the environment and never to that list, and Terraform manages it, so every plan reads it. The design worked exactly as intended: it failed at plan, before changing anything, and it failed on the boundary that exists to keep CI away from the secret key. Nothing in AWS was modified. Fixed by adding only that one ARN to the existing statement; the plan is +0 ~1 -0, one resource, one statement, statement set otherwise unchanged, verified from the plan JSON rather than from the diff text. The live policy was captured first as a rollback artifact. Worth noting the chicken-and-egg this exposes: the permission CI needs is granted by Terraform, and Terraform in CI cannot run without it, so an admin session has to apply this one.

checks.name: A CI deploy failed on two variables a gitignored file had been supplying
checks.detail: The public proof page merged and deploy-test failed at plan with 'No value for required variable', twice. The two new package-path variables were declared without defaults and given values in infrastructure/envs/test/terraform.tfvars, which is gitignored, so they existed on this workstation and never on a runner. Every other package-path variable carries a default pointing at the deterministic dist path, which is the convention this missed. Same shape as the parity mistake earlier: something true locally, read as true everywhere. Fixed by adding the two defaults. A new guard, scripts/lib/tf-var-supply.test.mjs, asserts that no test variable is left for a gitignored file to supply, and its third test replays the broken declaration to prove it catches it. The first draft of that guard was wrong twice and both errors are recorded in it: it checked production, which declares no defaults by design and is never deployed by this workflow, and it flagged empty defaults, which are a legitimate sentinel here since webauthn_rp_id defaults to empty so main.tf can derive it from app_origin's host. Checked against live AWS rather than assumed: WEBAUTHN_RP_ID survived the CI deploy as test.zoryvex.space, which is what proved the empty-default rule wrong.

checks.name: The public proof page is deployed, dark, and does not let a traversal past the authorizer
checks.detail: Plan +14 ~52 -0, which is two Lambdas at seven resources each plus every bundle rebuilt because packages/contracts changed, and the two scheduler policies that are always unknown at plan time. Apply clean, site sync 231 uploaded and 7 deleted of 272, /health smoke test passed, feature flags still matching Terraform. Verified against the running environment rather than the log. The feature is dark as designed: no pointer rows exist, so a fabricated id, an internal-looking id and the badge route all return an identical 404, 'No public proof page here', with no way to tell which reason applies. A path traversal was investigated properly rather than waved away after fetch() reported 200: fetch normalises '../' per the URL spec so the request never left the machine, and sending raw unnormalised paths showed API Gateway normalising them itself before routing. The security question was whether that normalisation could reach an authenticated route without a session, and it cannot — /billing, /admin/billing and /candidates/me each return 401 whether reached directly or through a traversal, so the authorizer applies to the resolved route. The 200 was API Gateway resolving to /health, which is public anyway. Copy confirmed served from the live JavaScript chunks on both routes: 'What this page does not tell you' and 'we will not say which' on /proof, and 'Publish a public proof page' and 'Turning this off destroys the link' on the profile.

checks.name: The evidence hierarchy is ordered by resistance to faking, founder-decided
checks.detail: The verification brief put peer verification near the top of its eight levels, which was harmless while the order was only a label. Ranking began using it on 2026-09-02, so a level's position now decides who an employer sees first, and under the brief's order a peer attestation would have outranked a machine-verified outcome: the most collusion-prone signal above the hardest to fake, inverting the brief's own stated preference for machine-verified outcome over opinion. The two halves of the brief disagreed once the order became load-bearing. Put to the founder with that consequence stated rather than resolved quietly, and they chose to keep the new order: claimed, peer verified, knowledge assessed, skill demonstrated, process observed, outcome verified, work corroborated, continuously verified. Peer verification is not demoted out of scepticism about colleagues; it is attributable testimony from somebody who proved control of an address at the organisation the work was done at, and it sits below the machine checks because a colleague can be mistaken, or a friend. A test asserts it can never outrank a machine-verified outcome, so this cannot drift back by accident, and reordering is now a founder decision with an entry in docs/DECISIONS.md, the same as a price, because it moves who gets seen.
